Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Magnetic Resonance
Silent Activatable Probe with Massive
Signal Amplification for Rapid Detection of Inflammation-Associated
Fibrogenesis
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Biomarker-specific molecular imaging is vital in precision medicine. However, a fundamental challenge of most molecular imaging methods is the difficulty of distinguishing specific molecular signal from nonspecific signal arising from the distribution of the molecular probe. This is even more pronounced in metabolically active organs such as the kidney and liver where the probe may concentrate prior to elimination. As a result, almost all molecular imaging relies on delayed imaging to achieve specificity, but this constrains clinical throughput and impedes rapid assessment of the diseased organ. Here, we report a magnetic resonance (MR) probe, Fe(II)-IAFP2, which combines 3 drivers of relaxivity enhancement to decouple disease specificity from probe distribution. Fe(II)-IAFP2 is MR-silent in its Fe(II) state, producing negligible MR signal even at high concentrations. In inflammatory, fibrogenic microenvironments common to many diseases, rapid oxidation to Fe(III) activates MR enhancement, while reversible aldehyde-mediated binding to remodeled extracellular matrix further amplifies relaxivity and promotes retention at the site of tissue injury. This dual activation–retention mechanism enables robust signal generation within minutes of administration. In mouse models of renal and liver fibrogenesis, Fe(II)-IAFP2 generated disease-associated MR contrast within minutes after intravenous administration. Together, this work demonstrates an effective strategy for rapid, activity-based molecular MR imaging through the combination of pathological activation and complementary tissue retention.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Photomediated Chromium-Catalyzed
Regio-, Diastereo-,
and Enantioselective Deoxygenative Coupling of Activated Allylic and
Propargylic Alcohols with Aldehydes
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Chromium-catalyzed asymmetric Nozaki–Hiyama–Kishi (NHK) reaction is a powerful tool for constructing synthetically valuable enantioenriched homoallylic alcohols and allenols. However, catalytic asymmetric NHK-type coupling of allylic or propargylic C–O electrophiles remains largely underdeveloped. Herein, we report a photomediated chromium-catalyzed deoxygenative coupling of activated allylic and propargylic alcohols with aldehydes, enabling the synthesis of a variety of chiral homoallylic alcohols with wide structural diversity and allenols. The reactions were performed under mild conditions, and a wide range of synthetically useful functional groups was found to be well tolerated. Importantly, this method provides a straightforward way for the construction of homoallylic alcohols bearing a chiral quaternary carbon center with high ee and dr. Furthermore, stereodivergent access to all four homoallylic alcohol stereoisomers is realized through orthogonal combinations of Z/E-configured allylic alcohols and R/S-configured ligands. Combined experimental and computational mechanistic studies provided insight into the key catalytic intermediate and the origin of stereocontrol.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title: Anti -Dihydroxylation-Enabled Dual-Resolution Profiling and Imaging of Fatty Acid C═C Bond Isomers
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Lipids are essential for membrane structure, signaling, and stress adaptation. Their diverse biological roles are largely dictated by the presence of C═C bonds in unsaturated fatty acids (FAs), which vary in both position and geometry. However, unambiguous characterization and in situ mapping of these two structural features have remained longstanding analytical challenges. Here, we present a stereochemistry-preserved chemical derivatization strategy coupled with trapped ion mobility spectrometry-tandem MS (TIMS-MS/MS), enabling complete resolution of both FA C═C bond position and geometry within a single workflow. This approach facilitates rapid and quantitative profiling of dynamic cis–trans isomerization in bacteria under diverse stress conditions and, notably, reveals a previously unrecognized dose-dependent antibiotic adaptation mechanism in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a multidrug-resistant pathogen. To translate this strategy to spatially resolved analyses, we developed an in situ derivatization workflow for mass spectrometry imaging, which uncovers the spatial heterogeneity of FA isomers in proximally cocultured, clinically relevant polymicrobial pathogens. These findings highlight colony-specific spatial dynamics of cis and trans lipid isomers and suggest lipid-mediated metabolic interactions between co-occurring microbial species. Together, this integrated platform enables both quantitative and spatial interrogation of lipid isomerization, providing new opportunities to systematically investigate its roles in microbial physiology, pathogenesis, and beyond.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Simultaneous
Selective Recognition of Two Different
Anions within a Hydrogen/Halogen-Bonding Cage
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The search for selective anion receptors that can function in water is a longstanding challenge in supramolecular chemistry, motivated by anions’ fundamental roles (and potential applications) in biological, environmental, and industrial processes. Here, we incorporate halogen and hydrogen bond donors into an easy-to-prepare organic cage molecule and demonstrate that this can bind anions at either or both of a halogen-bonding pocket and hydrogen-bonding pockets depending on the nature of the anions and the solvent. The halogen-bonding pocket comprising six bromopyridinium donors is a potent host for iodide anions and can selectively bind this guest in water as strongly as biological iodide binders (Ka = 43,000 M–1 measured by 1H NMR spectroscopy) with the exclusion of other halide anions. In DMSO/water mixtures, the hydrogen-bonding pockets are able to recognize chloride anions, resulting in the formation of mixed anion iodide/chloride complexes with an iodide bound in the center of the cage and chlorides in the peripheral binding sites. This demonstrates the exquisite selectivity afforded by halogen-bonding systems and reveals a general route to a range of supramolecular anion hosts that bind multiple guests in different locations.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Functional Specialization
of Coordination Spheres
Enables Site-Selective Aromatic C–H Isotope Exchange in Ni
Single-Atom Catalysts
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Engineering single-atom catalysts has predominantly focused on tailoring the primary coordination sphere, whereas whether distinct coordination spheres can be endowed with independent catalytic functions remains largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate the functional specialization of coordination spheres by constructing a phosphorus-modified Ni–N2O2 single-atom catalyst for site-selective C–H deuteration. Advanced spectroscopic characterizations and theoretical calculations show that phosphorus is incorporated outside the preserved primary Ni–N2O2 coordination environment and support an O-linked phosphorus environment as a preferential second-sphere motif. This architecture decouples substrate recognition from catalytic activation. Specifically, second-sphere phosphorus selectively recognizes and anchors the amino group of haloanilines to dictate deuteration site selectivity, whereas the preserved primary Ni–N2O2 coordination sphere promotes H2 activation and undergoes H2-assisted regeneration following D2O-induced hydroxylation, facilitated by P–O–Ni electronic communication, thereby sustaining efficient catalytic turnover. Consequently, the catalyst achieves highly site-selective C–H deuteration of chloro-, bromo-, and iodoanilines using H2 and D2O while completely preserving carbon–halogen bonds, whereas the phosphorus-free analogue exhibits negligible activity. This work identifies the structural origin and catalytic function of second-sphere phosphorus and establishes functional specialization of coordination spheres as a general design principle for independently programming substrate recognition and catalytic turnover in single-atom catalysis.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Molecular
Mechanophores Based on Stress-Enhanced Exciton
Transition between Phosphorescent Probes and Polymer Matrix
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Mechanophores provide an in situ and remote tool for quantifying invisible stress in polymers by photonic signals, offering distinct advantages for stress distribution analysis of large-area surfaces and instrument-free stress observation. However, achieving an ideal mechanophore that integrates with sensitive, reversible, and molecular-level stress sensing is attractive yet challenging. Here, we report practical guidance for developing ideal mechanophores that promote the molecular probe’s exciton transition for room-temperature phosphorescence (RTP) under stress, through the “assisted lowest triplet (T1) state” of the adjacent polymer chain. Systematic analyses of numerous organic probes reveal that a small energy gap (ΔEM &lt; 0.4 eV) between the probe’s lowest singlet (S1) and the polymer’s T1 states is an empirical guideline for stress-enhanced RTP. The probe-doped polymer system demonstrates not only a remarkable increase in RTP intensity of over 2000-fold upon 160 MPa but also a low stress threshold of ∼2 MPa, which is robust under 0–10 MPa cyclic pressure loading/unloading over 500 cycles. Such RTP mechanophores enable noninvasive, reversible, and molecular-level stress detection in polymers. Their doped polymers have shown potential applications in various fields for real-time sensing of stress and its uneven distribution through visual afterglow.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Linker Steric Hindrance-Induced
Defect Engineering
Enables Oxygen Vacancy-Rich MOFs for Pollutant Degradation
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The widespread contamination of water by emerging contaminants (ECs) demands the development of efficient remediation technologies. Although advanced oxidation processes reliant on reactive oxygen species (ROS) show promise, they typically depend on energy- or reagent-intensive activation methods. Here, we introduce a linker steric hindrance-induced defect engineering (LSH-DE) strategy for metal–organic frameworks, which enables catalytic ROS generation using molecular oxygen (O2) as a benign terminal oxidant at ambient temperature and pressure. By systematically modulating the steric bulk of organic linkers, we precisely create missing-linker defects and direct the formation of oxygen vacancy (Vo) in robust Ce-UiO-66 during a rapid 15 min synthesis. Spectroscopic and computational analyses confirm that these oxygen vacancies promote O2 adsorption and activation to yield superoxide radicals (•O2–). The optimized catalyst, Ce-UiO-66-(CH3)2, demonstrates superior activity in degrading ubiquitous ECs without requiring external energy inputs or chemical mediators. Furthermore, integration of Ce-UiO-66-(CH3)2 into a membrane-based recirculating flow-through system enabled sustained water treatment, maintaining &gt;90% BPA removal over 48 h with a high water permeance of 101.5 L m–2 h–1 bar–1. This work presents a general and sustainable approach for designing catalytic defects in MOFs, advancing the development of green, next-generation water purification technologies.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Hybrid Weakly Coordinated
Solvents for Fast-Charging
and Wide-Temperature Sodium-Ion Full Batteries
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The application of sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) in wide-temperature and fast-charging scenarios is severely constrained by the performance limitations of electrolytes. Conventional ester-based electrolytes struggle to simultaneously achieve high ionic conductivity, low desolvation energy, and excellent interfacial stability. Herein, we propose a hybrid solvent system comprising ethyl propionate and ethoxy(pentafluoro)cyclotriphosphazene (PFPN), aiming to synergistically enhance the rate capability and temperature adaptability of SIBs. The relatively weak coordination ability of both solvents effectively promotes anion participation in solvation structure, significantly lowering the Na+ desolvation energy barrier and inducing the formation of stable, inorganic-rich electrode/electrolyte interphases. Meanwhile, the dual-solvent combination increases the diversity of solvation configurations and reduces ion clustering, thereby enhancing ionic conductivity. The intrinsic nonflammability and excellent film-forming ability of PFPN further enhance safety and synergistically strengthen interfacial stability. Therefore, Prussian blue||hard carbon full cells operate stably over a wide temperature range from −50 to 100 °C. Notably, ampere-hour-level pouch cells deliver a capacity retention of 86.3% after 300 cycles at 25 °C and maintain stable operation for over 100 cycles even at −20 and 80 °C. This solvent synergy strategy offers a practical new pathway for the development of electrolytes for SIBs in extreme environments.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Ammonia-Driven Nanoscale
Surface Restructuring of
Copper Catalysts during Nitrate Reduction Reaction
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The electrolyte and applied potential are known to impact a catalyst’s structure and performance, yet the role of reaction intermediates and products in driving surface evolution remains largely unexplored. Here, using electrochemical atomic force microscopy, we show that the dynamic restructuring of copper (Cu) surfaces during nitrate reduction reaction (NO3RR) directly correlates with the rate and selectivity of ammonia (NH3) formation. At moderate overpotentials, where nitrite formation dominates, lateral expansion of Cu terraces is observed, whereas rapid NH3 formation at higher cathodic potentials induces Cu adislands enriched in low-coordinated step sites, revealing distinct restructuring pathways that accompany the transition from nitrite- to ammonia-selective NO3RR. These transformations are rationalized by an NH3-mediated Cu dissolution-redeposition mechanism. Our results identify reaction products as active modulators of catalyst surface structure, establishing a framework for understanding reaction-driven catalyst restructuring and enabling in situ control of catalyst surfaces through the interfacial reaction environment.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Empowering HFIP as
a Radical Trifluoromethylating
Reagent by Photoelectrochemical Iron Catalysis
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The development of practical synthetic methods for incorporating trifluoromethyl (CF3) groups into organic scaffolds is of paramount importance in medicinal chemistry, as such modifications profoundly modulate the physicochemical properties of drug candidates. 1,1,1,3,3,3-Hexafluoro-2-propanol (HFIP) is widely utilized as a unique solvent in synthetic chemistry and also represents a promising CF3 source due to its high availability and low cost. Here we report an unprecedented photoelectrochemical iron-catalyzed protocol for radical trifluoromethylation that employs commercially accessible HFIP as the CF3 radical precursor. This method enables efficient trifluoromethylation of unactivated arenes, heteroarenes, and alkenes with a broad substrate scope and excellent functional group tolerance. Notably, this photoelectrocatalytic system is readily scalable for practical synthetic applications, and its utility has been demonstrated in the trifluoromethylation of peptides, allowing preferential modification of tryptophan residues in a chemoselective fashion.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Interfacial
Confinement Enables Conformal IrOx Nanofilms for Low-Ir-Loading
PEM Water Electrolysis
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Terawatt-scale deployment of proton-exchange membrane water electrolyzers (PEMWEs) requires low iridium (Ir) loading, which disrupts the catalyst layer’s in-plane electronic percolation network and severely degrades performance. Here, we overcome this bottleneck via an interfacial confinement strategy that electrostatically enriches cationic Ir intermediates on the negatively charged, oxygen-deficient TiOx surface, thereby redirecting Ir deposition from three-dimensional island growth to a two-dimensional conformal film on TiO2 supports. The resulting IrOx-NF@TiO2 catalyst with low Ir packing density maintains long-range in-plane electron percolation, reducing reliance on the high Ir loading typically required by conventional IrOx nanoparticle catalysts to establish quasi-continuous conductive pathways. At a loading of 0.166 mgIr cm−2, blade-coated membrane electrode assemblies incorporating this architecture feature ∼7 μm-thick catalyst layers with an Ir packing density of only ∼0.25 gIr cm–3, allowing an ∼84% reduction in Ir use while achieving performance comparable to that of commercial IrO2. This work highlights the potential of supported conformal IrOx catalysts as competitive candidates for next-generation low-Ir PEMWEs.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Acetaldehyde-Mediated
Direct Conversion of Air to
Nitric Acid
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The sustainable synthesis of nitric acid (HNO3) directly from air via N2 oxidation is a dream reaction but remains a long-standing challenge, owing to formidable thermodynamic and kinetic barriers. Here, we report a photoassisted thermocatalytic strategy in which acetaldehyde as a key medium enables efficient N2 oxidation to HNO3 under mild conditions. Acetaldehyde is oxidized to peracetic acid over 316L stainless steel, which subsequently generates radicals (CH3COOO•) under visible-light irradiation. These CH3COOO• radicals are highly reactive and can oxidize N2 at 200 °C and near-ambient pressures (1–5 bar), affording an HNO3 formation rate of 110.8 μmol h–1 with a concentration of 13,961 ppm and an N2 conversion of 0.45% within 2 h─approximately 2 to 4 orders of magnitude higher than previously reported systems. Notably, the kinetic irrelevance of H2O enables operation in a gas-phase flow configuration, allowing continuous and stable HNO3 production and gram-scale accumulation at the laboratory scale. This work introduces a groundbreaking reaction paradigm that couples organic radical chemistry and surface catalysis, offering a scalable and energy-efficient pathway for the green synthesis of HNO3.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
A Crystalline LaCl3 Reinforced Amorphous
Oxyhalide Electrolyte for Thermally Stable All-Solid-State Batteries
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>All-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) are a promising next-generation energy storage technology, but their development is often constrained by the thermal instability and high cost of solid-state electrolytes (SSEs). Amorphous oxyhalide electrolytes, while mechanically deformable, are particularly susceptible to thermal degradation. Here, we report a novel and cost-effective composite SSE fabricated by embedding LaCl3 nanocrystals within an amorphous Li–Al–O–Cl (LAOC) matrix. This unique architecture synergistically combines the high ionic conductivity of the amorphous phase with the enhanced thermal and mechanical robustness imparted by the crystalline phase. The resulting Li–La–Al–O–Cl electrolyte achieves a high room-temperature ionic conductivity exceeding 1 mS cm–1 and demonstrates exceptional thermal stability, remaining a solid powder at 150 °C, a temperature at which the baseline LAOC melts. This enhanced thermal and thermo-mechanical integrity, combined with excellent deformability, enables superior interfacial contact and stability with cathodes. The Li–La–Al–O–Cl-based ASSBs maintain stable operation at 80 °C, in stark contrast to the rapid failure of LAOC-based cells. This strategy of reinforcing a soft amorphous matrix with a rigid crystalline offers a new pathway for designing thermally robust, high-performance, and commercially viable SSEs.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
General Synthesis of
Functionalized 1,3-Diamines from
Azoarenes and Enoates via Electrochemical Annulation and N–N
Bond Cleavage Followed by Chemical Reduction
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Despite the widespread utility of N-substituted 1,3-diamines across numerous fields, their selective synthesis directly from readily available feedstocks remains a long-standing challenge. In this context, we report a room-temperature electrochemical protocol for the synthesis of both symmetrical and unsymmetrical N,N′-disubstituted 1,3-diamines through electrochemical transformation of azoarenes with enoates, followed by convergent reduction of the resulting β-amino amides. This method features broad substrate scope, operational simplicity, no need for noble transition-metal catalysts, and high chemoselectivity. Mechanistic studies indicate that the reaction is initiated by the reduction of azoarenes, facilitated by HCOOH, while Zn2+ ions leached from anodic oxidation serve as a Lewis acid to promote intramolecular cyclization via ester amidation. Subsequent cathodic reduction drives N–N bond cleavage to afford the β-amino amide intermediates, thereby endowing azoarenes with dual-nitrogen synthon capability. This work provides a practical platform for the general synthesis of N,N′-difunctionalized 1,3-diamines and convenient late-stage structural editing of biomedicals.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Solvent/Anion
Codepleted Solvation Engineering Enables
Low-Coordination Electrolytes for High-Energy and Low-Temperature
Sodium-Ion Pouch Cells
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Widespread deployment of sodium-ion batteries demands both high energy density and reliable low-temperature (LT) operation, but is constrained by a persistent trade-off between high-voltage stability (cathode/electrolyte) and LT ion-transport kinetics. Herein, we report a solvent/anion codepleted solvation engineering strategy to construct low-coordination electrolytes through competitive anion complexation mediated by a bulky electron-deficient additive, TMSB (tris(trimethylsilyl)borate). We reveal that TMSB preferentially complexes with PF6– to suppress direct anion-Na+ coordination, while its bulky steric backbone disrupts conventional ion-pair networks and restricts excessive solvent-Na+ coordination. This strategy fundamentally boosts ionic conductivity (from 2.41 to 5.34 mS cm–1) and lowers the desolvation energy barrier (from 44.82 to 33.97 kJ mol–1). Moreover, such a strategy enables a high-modulus (2.7 GPa), inorganic-rich cathode-electrolyte interphase (CEI), which can not only mitigate surface degradation, but also suppress bulk phase transitions of cathode materials. Consequently, the electrolyte demonstrates broad compatibility across diverse cathodes (NFM, NVP, and P2-NNMO) under extreme voltage (up to 4.5 V) and temperature (−40 to 25 °C) conditions. Remarkably, the scaled-up 6.8 Ah pouch cell achieves a record-high energy density of 200 Wh kg–1 at 25 °C, while maintaining 162 Wh kg–1 even at −20 °C, offering a generalizable molecular paradigm for extreme-environment energy storage.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Role of (Co)substrate
Coordination to Iron in Activating
Its Two-Electron Reduction of Dioxygen: Mechanism of Pterin Activation
in Tryptophan Hydroxylase
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Many O2-activating mononuclear nonheme iron enzymes require substrate or cofactor/cosubstrate coordination to iron to form the key peroxy-bridged intermediate necessary for catalysis with no net change in the iron redox state. The role of (co)substrate coordination, however, remained unclear. Here, we leverage a pterin-dependent enzyme, tryptophan hydroxylase, for which cosubstrate (pterin) coordination can be experimentally controlled by the absence and presence of substrate, to explicitly determine the role of pterin coordination in O2 binding and peroxo formation. EPR, absorption, circular dichroism, and magnetic circular dichroism spectroscopies on the {FeNO}7 analog of the unobservable {FeO2}8 intermediate without and with pterin coordination demonstrate that pterin coordination induces new absorption bands and enhances NO affinity by 3.6 kcal mol–1 at 277 K. These new bands are pterin-to-iron ligand-to-metal charge-transfer transitions that compensate the electron donation from iron to NO upon NO binding. Extension of our findings on {FeNO}7 to {FeO2}8 evidences that pterin coordination stabilizes O2 binding and facilitates the two-electron transfer from pterin to {FeO2}8 to reduce the transition-state barrier for peroxo formation by 12.7 kcal mol–1, corresponding to a 1010 increase in reaction rate. The electron transfer pathways established herein underscore a unified mechanism for the pterin-dependent, α-ketoglutarate-dependent, extradiol, and intradiol dioxygenase families of mononuclear nonheme iron enzymes through which (co)substrate coordination enhances O2 binding via one-electron transfer within {FeO2}8 and two-electron donation from the (co)substrate (one to bound O2 and one to iron) to generate the peroxo species with no net redox change on the iron.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Breaking the “Micro-Size
Inversion”
Paradox via a Surface-Chemistry-Driven Molecular Sieving Membrane
for Ambient Lithium–Air Batteries
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Lithium–air batteries suffer from moisture-induced parasitic reactions and electrolyte evaporation in ambient air. A fundamental challenge is the “micro-size inversion” paradox, where H2O (0.275 nm) is smaller than O2 (0.346 nm), rendering conventional size-based sieving ineffective. Here, we report a composite membrane composed of polydimethylsiloxane and fluorinated vinyl-functionalized covalent organic framework (COF-VF) to break this selectivity barrier. By grafting 1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorodecyl groups onto a vinyl-functionalized covalent organic framework (COF-V), we establish a surface-chemistry-driven sieving mechanism. This design creates a molecular-level hydrogen-bond-repellent barrier that specifically inhibits polar H2O penetration while maintaining high nonpolar O2 flux, effectively decoupling the permeability-hydrophobicity trade-off. Molecular dynamics simulations corroborate this mechanism, demonstrating that the COF-VF exhibits significantly reduced adsorption affinity toward H2O compared to the pristine COF-V. In 40% RH ambient air, the battery equipped with this membrane delivers a discharge capacity of 3596 mAh g–1 and sustains cycling for 2700 h (270 cycles), a 10.8-fold improvement over unprotected cells. Advanced characterizations via DRT and DEMS confirm that the membrane promotes reversible Li2O2 formation and significantly suppresses LiOH accumulation. This work provides a multiscale strategy for molecular-level selective separation in practical energy storage.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Specific Amino Acid
Imaging of Protein Condensates
in Live Cells by Stimulated Raman Scattering Microscopy
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Intracellular protein condensates formed by liquid–liquid phase separation have gained increasing attention in recent years due to their key roles in many physiological and pathological processes. However, fluorescence imaging of protein condensates is limited by the bulky fluorescent tags that could perturb the protein localization and interaction. Imaging techniques that can visualize protein condensates in live cells with minimal perturbations remain lacking. Here, we develop a strategy to image intracellular protein condensates by coupling stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscopy to specific amino acid labeling. Different types of amino acids are found to exhibit distinct incorporation patterns in the live cells. By metabolic labeling of deuterated tyrosine-d4 and arginine-d7, ALS-related fused in sarcoma (FUS) protein condensates can be visualized with a high specificity. In addition, two-color pulse-chase imaging reveals protein translation arrest in FUS condensates under stress conditions. Furthermore, heterogeneous tyrosine phosphorylation is imaged in live cells and FUS condensates based on the Raman blue shift of phosphorylated tyrosine-d4. Thus, our technique to image specific amino acids by SRS provides a new platform to visualize the metabolic turnover and post-translational modifications of protein condensates in live cells with minimal perturbation.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Low-Temperature-Mediated
Lamellar–Micelle Assembly
of Wrinkled Mesoporous Carbon Nanospheres with Aligned Pores and High
Interconnectivity
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Mesoporous structures with highly permeable channels are of great significance for fast diffusion; however, the delicate engineering of straightforward pores remains quite limited, with most of mesostructures are tortuous pores derived from spherical micelle assembly. Herein, we explore a novel lamellar–micelle assembly approach that enables to generate a type of wrinkled mesoporous carbon nanospheres with highly interconnected divergent mesopores. In place of the conventional spherical micelles, the key for controlling such unusual assembly is determined by the construction of laminar micelles (copolymer L121/F127 composite) and heterogeneous growth on sedimented F127 seeds at a low temperature of 5 °C. The fabricated wrinkled mesoporous carbon nanospheres after template removal possess a particle size at ∼910 nm, a high surface area of 315 m2 g–1, a uniform pore size at 36 nm, as well as radial mesochannels with high interconnectivity up to 96%. Further regulation on the reaction temperature and template ratio allows for a high tunability over the pore size and wrinkle degree. When employed as a sodium storage anode, the radially aligned large-pore structure drastically facilitates charge transport and electrolyte penetration, thus delivering rate capability (142 mAh g–1 at 10 A g–1) and long-term cyclability (90.5% retention after 1000 cycles at 2 A g–1) compared to commercial hard carbon. Our work underscores a particular assembly pathway through lamellar micelles as an effective approach for building up ultrafast mesopore highways toward promising diffusion-related applications.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
A Single Water Molecule
Drives a 20-Fold Acceleration
in the Gas-Phase Reaction of Iodide with Ozone
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Iodine chemistry has an outsized role in the atmosphere and environment due to its highly reactive nature. Unlike chlorine and bromine, around 80% of atmospheric iodine is emitted directly from the ocean through the reaction of iodide and ozone at the sea surface. Uncertainties remain, however, in the effects of hydration, salinity, temperature, and other factors on this globally significant reaction. Using linear ion-trap mass spectrometry, a single water molecule is shown here to provide a 23 (±6)-fold acceleration to the rate of iodide oxidation. The first step in reaction of both I– and I–·H2O with ozone is oxidation to IO– with subsequent fast reactions to yield IO3–. No evidence is found for direct routes from I–·H2O to IO2– nor any incorporation of the water oxygen into ionic products. Ab initio calculations show that the initial rate-determining step for both reactions proceeds on the singlet surface with water playing an active role to lower the barrier through hydrogen bonding. Kinetic modeling based on the computed energetics is in excellent agreement with experimental measurements and enables extrapolation of this reaction to lower temperatures relevant to polar regions and the ozone layer. This analysis shows that (i) I– may outcompete I• for ozone destruction as temperature decreases, and (ii) I–·H2O reacts more than an order of magnitude faster than I• over 350 to 230 K. This work demonstrates that iodide has a previously underappreciated role in multiphase ozone destruction in the atmosphere and lays the foundation for understanding microscopic environmental influences in salt clusters and nanodroplets.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Control of Charge Carrier
Dynamics and Bandgap Renormalization
in CdS Quantum Dot Hybrids by Interface Polarity
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Charge carrier dynamics in wurtzite CdS quantum dots (QDs) form the basis for applications in optoelectronics and photocatalysis. We demonstrate that the quantum dynamics, energy gaps, and energy level alignments at CdS QD interfaces can be controlled by the polarity of the CdS QD surface. By performing nonadiabatic molecular dynamics simulations within a density-functional tight-binding framework, we demonstrate a strong dependence of photoinitiated processes in CdS QDs/graphene nanoribbon (GNR) hybrids on interface polarity. At room temperature, hole transfer is accelerated by a factor of 2 and exciton lifetime is enhanced by nearly an order of magnitude when the CdS QD surface is switched from polar to nonpolar. Remarkably, the interfacial bandgap for the polar QD/GNR hybrid is reduced to half upon heating from 0 K to room temperature, while it remains nearly unchanged for the nonpolar hybrid. At an intermediate temperature, the ultrafast charge separation is maintained; however, charge recombination shows the opposite trend relative to room temperature. The polar interface exhibits a longer lifetime than the nonpolar interface, due to weakened electron–phonon Fröhlich interaction and decreased gap renormalization. The strong and highly nonlinear dependence of bandgap renormalization and carrier dynamics on temperature in the polar QD/GNR hybrid is associated with significant structural reconstruction, which is absent in the nonpolar counterpart. The demonstrated control of excited-state processes by interface polarity and the strong dependence of the dynamics and energy level alignment on temperature provide key fundamental insights for informed design of modern materials for optoelectronics and energy conversion.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Mapping the Slow Propagation
of Disorder across a
Photoreceptor’s Tertiary Structure with Time-Resolved Crystallography
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Order–disorder transitions allow many proteins to shift between compact and flexible/unfolded states, thereby acting as structural switches that regulate catalysis, signaling, recognition, and allostery. We applied time-resolved serial oscillation crystallography to establish the structural kinetics of the light-triggered order–disorder transition of an animal-like cryptochrome as a six-second-long molecular movie with near-atomic all-residue spatial resolution and millisecond temporal resolution. Our 29 structural snapshots mapped the propagation of disorder across the tertiary structure motifs of a cryptochrome’s C-terminal region, triggered by a single broken D321–R492 salt bridge. The order–disorder transition followed a nucleation-propagation mechanism reminiscent of helix–coil dynamics and proceeded over up to five seconds, with regions distal to the D321–R492 trigger initially undergoing slow zero-order disordering before switching to first-order unfolding kinetics. Our per-residue density analysis provides a detailed structural-kinetic basis for understanding how order–disorder transitions emerge through directional propagation across protein tertiary structures, as occurring in signaling and many other biological systems.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Electron-Catalyzed
Supramolecular Assembly with High
Efficiency, Robustness, and Versatility
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Although catalysis is widely exploited by nature to orchestrate noncovalent supramolecular assembly and build up complex living systems, its utilization in synthetic chemistry has conventionally been limited to accelerating covalent reactions. Consequently, the development of artificial systems for catalytic assembly remains a formidable and largely unexplored challenge. Here, we present a rationally designed strategy of electron-catalyzed supramolecular assembly, wherein the electron acts as an efficient, robust, and versatile catalyst to accelerate the formation of a donor–acceptor complex. Optimization of the elementary steps and intermediate stability yields an efficient catalytic cycle, furnishing the process with both a high turnover number and operational robustness in open air. Furthermore, the electron catalysis can be readily triggered by diverse external stimuli─including electricity, light, and mechanical force─enabling precise spatiotemporal control over the assembly process and near-quantitative synthesis of supramolecular complexes. Collectively, this work establishes a well-elucidated strategy of catalytic assembly with remarkable practicality, advancing the frontiers of noncovalent synthetic chemistry.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Reprogramming ThDP-Dependent
Enzyme for Intermolecular
[3 + 2] Annulation via a Homoenolate Intermediate
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Thiamine diphosphate (ThDP)-dependent enzymes are versatile biocatalysts for carbon–carbon bond formation, yet their catalytic repertoire has been largely confined to linear homologation and intramolecular cyclizations that rely on single-site reactive intermediates such as the Breslow or ketyl radical species. Intermolecular annulation─a powerful strategy for constructing cyclic architectures─has remained elusive within this enzyme class. Here, we report the first intermolecular [3 + 2] annulation catalyzed by a ThDP-dependent enzyme, achieved through a homoenolate-mediated nucleophilic addition pathway. A phylogeny-guided enzyme mining identified a previously uncharacterized enzyme from Variovorax boronicumulans(ThDP-5), and subsequent protein engineering yielded the F484S variant, which exhibits markedly enhanced activity and exquisite stereocontrol. This biocatalytic system exhibits a broad substrate scope (30 examples), accommodating diverse substituted cinnamaldehydes and isatins to afford chiral spirooxindole lactones with excellent stereoselectivity (up to &gt; 20:1 dr and 99% ee). Preparative-scale reactions (2 mmol) validate its synthetic utility. This work expands ThDP-dependent biocatalysis to intermolecular annulations, providing a robust and selective platform for the construction of pharmaceutically relevant spirocyclic architectures.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Direct Observation
of Chirality-Dependent Berry Curvature
Dipole via Cross-Axial Nonlinear Hall Effect in Trigonal Te
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Quantum geometric quantities, such as Berry curvature (BC) and quantum metric, are known to govern the physical and topological properties of materials, making access to these quantities critically important for the comprehensive understanding of the materials. Chiral crystals offer a natural platform in which structural handedness can control quantum geometry and nonlinear transport, but direct experimental access to the quantum geometric quantities has remained elusive. Here, we show that trigonal tellurium (Te) hosts an enantiomer-dependent Berry curvature dipole (BCD) that can be accessed through the measurement of the cross-axial nonlinear Hall effect (NHE), unlike in previously studied in-plane configurations, where the BCD contribution vanishes. Angle-resolved measurements on left- and right-handed Te devices reveal a second-order transverse response whose sign reverses with crystal chirality. The extracted cross-axial nonlinear susceptibility, χyxz, exceeds the in-plane susceptibility, χxxx, by more than two-fold, indicating a strong BCD-driven contribution. First-principles calculations attribute this behavior to a topologically nontrivial hedgehog-like BC texture near the H points and predict a BCD that reverses sign between opposite enantiomers, consistent with experiment. These results establish cross-axial nonlinear Hall transport as a symmetry-selective probe of chirality-controlled quantum geometry in tellurium and related chiral materials.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Polarization-Controlled
Dual-Mode Switching in van
der Waals α-In2Se3 Memristors for
Multitime-Scale Reservoir Computing
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Electrochemical-metallization (ECM) memristors can implement both nonvolatile memory switching and volatile threshold switching, making them attractive for neuromorphic and reservoir computing; however, the stochastic formation of metallic filaments causes variability in the threshold voltage and switching instability. Here, we report a van der Waals α-In2Se3-based ferroelectric-semiconductor ECM (FeS-ECM) memristor in which a bidirectionally polarized α-In2Se3 layer is inserted between the inert electrode and the switching layer. The out-of-plane ferroelectric polarization, programmed through a decoupled in-plane poling terminal, deterministically selects within the low-compliance operating regime between nonvolatile bipolar memory switching and volatile unipolar threshold switching within a single device, with a coefficient of variation in the set voltage of 4.7% and stable operation over more than 9000 cycles. Exploiting these two modes, a single α-In2Se3 platform exhibits both the volatile reservoir dynamics and the nonvolatile conductance modulation required for the readout weights of a physical reservoir-computing system, in which the pulse width electrically programs multiple relaxation time constants. This pulse-width multitime scale reconfigurability enables efficient temporal information processing, demonstrated through MNIST classification and chaotic time-series prediction.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Switching of Exciton-Polaritons
in Covalent Organic
Framework-Based Optical Resonators through Interaction with the Molecular
Environment
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We report a demonstration of a covalent organic framework (COF) integrated into an optical cavity for the realization of exciton–polaritons and their reversible switching through changes in the surrounding molecular environment. Films of COF nanoplates were integrated into Fabry–Pérot resonators engineered to achieve spectral matching between cavity modes and COF excitonic transitions, yielding strong light–matter coupling with a Rabi splitting above 300 meV. The cavity architecture preserves accessibility of the porous framework, enabling interaction with guest molecules. The potential of this interplay is shown by exposing the resonators to water vapor, which induces both a redshift and a pronounced reduction of the COF optical absorption. The observed hypochromic effect drives a reversible shift from strong to weak coupling, effectively switching exciton–polaritons on and off, as guest molecules are desorbed from or adsorbed in the reticular material host. The process is reversible upon desorption, with preservation of structural and optical integrity. These results establish COFs as a versatile platform for chemically tunable polaritonic systems, opening avenues for responsive photonic devices, sensing, and control of light–matter interactions in nanostructured materials.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Shield-and-Amplify
Nanoparticle Vaccines Retune Immunodominance
for Broad Protection against SARS-CoV-2
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Antigenic variation severely constrains the durability and breadth of vaccine-induced protection against rapidly evolving viruses. Although conserved epitopes can support cross-variant immunity, antibody responses to viral glycoproteins are often biased toward exposed, mutable immunodominant epitopes, leaving conserved protective sites subdominant. We previously identified a cryptic, conserved class 5 epitope (the 6D6/7D6 epitope) on the SARS-CoV-2 receptor-binding domain (RBD) capable of eliciting broad cross-neutralization. Here, we present a modular “shield-and-amplify” nanoparticle vaccination strategy to redirect immunodominance toward this subdominant epitope. We engineered site-specific N-linked glycans─alongside the native N343 glycan to mask variable immunodominant regions while preserving accessibility to the class 5 epitope. The resulting glycan-masked RBD antigen (RGM) was displayed on p239 nanoparticles via nanobody-mediated assembly, yielding multivalent RGM@p239 immunogens. Antigenic profiling revealed that glycan shielding preserved recognition by 6D6 and 7D6 antibodies while reducing binding of representative class 1–4 antibodies by at least 80%. In immunized animals, RGM@p239 enriched 7D6-competitive serum antibodies blocking approximately 70–80% of serum binding to RGM and broadened cross-variant neutralization against 8 representative variant strains, including detectable activity against Omicron lineages. Furthermore, RGM@p239 reduced disease severity after Omicron EG.1 challenge in a hamster model. These results support a model in which glycan shielding and nanoparticle multivalency act as complementary immune-focusing modules: shielding attenuates competing responses, while multivalency amplifies responses to conserved subdominant epitopes. This study establishes a nanovaccine design strategy to address antigenic variation by focusing immunity on conserved viral vulnerabilities.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Ultrasound-Responsive
Electroactive Polyetheretherketone
Scaffold Promotes Bioenergetic Bone Regeneration by Regulating Mitochondrial
Permeability Transition Pores
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Mitochondrial dysfunction and energy metabolic imbalance in senescent bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) are critical pathological foundations for senile bone regeneration. Existing therapeutic strategies suffer from a lack of active mitochondrial bioenergetic driving forces, failing to effectively reverse energy metabolic suppression of senescent BMSCs. Here, an ultrasound-activated electroactive scaffold was constructed by anchoring barium titanate-transition metal carbide (MXene@BaTiO3) heterojunctions on the surface of polyetheretherketone (PEEK) to reactivate mitochondrial energy metabolism and promote bone regeneration under senescence-associated bone loss conditions. These heterojunctions adhere to BMSC membranes and generate electrical stimulation upon ultrasound stimulation, which significantly inhibits abnormal opening of mitochondrial permeability transition pores (mPTP), reduces leakage of mtDNA and Cyt c, and maintains membrane potential stability. Mechanistic investigations reveal that electrical stimulation activates the PI3K/Akt/MDM2 signaling axis to promote the degradation of accumulated p53, which relieves the competitive binding of p53 to TRAP1, thereby restoring TRAP1-CypD-mediated mPTP gating and mitochondrial homeostasis. Consequently, this ultrasound-activated electroactive scaffold drives mitochondrial energy metabolism and osteogenic differentiation of senescence-like BMSCs in vitro, which is further confirmed in a rat model. These results demonstrate the potential of this electroactive scaffold as a regulator of mitochondrial energy metabolism for senescence-associated bone regeneration.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Chronic Stress-Triggerable
Nanoprodrugs Ameliorate
Metabolic Abnormalities Driven by Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Adrenal Axis
Dysregulation in Early Alzheimer’s Disease
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Chronic stress-induced dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis is a crucial early risk factor that triggers brain energy metabolism disorders to accelerate the onset and progression of Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Herein, an amphiphilic precursor conjugate of ginsenoside Rc (Rc) covalently linked with a reactive oxygen species-sensitive thioketo bond is constructed to form stimuli-responsive prodrug assemblies, which are further modified with the TGN-Tet1 dual-ligand fusion peptide TPL to obtain a chronic stress-triggerable programmed nanoprodrug (TLRN). Following TPL-mediated blood-brain barrier penetration and neuronal preferential targeting, nanoprodrugs specifically disintegrate to selectively release active Rc in the chronic stress-induced excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) microenvironment. Benefiting from the restoration of HPA axis homeostasis by normalizing glucocorticoid receptor nuclear translocation, TLRN treatment exhibits multifaceted rectification of cerebral metabolic abnormalities, including enhancing glucose uptake, promoting oxidative phosphorylation, and mitigating mitochondrial dysfunction. In young amyloid precursor protein/presenilin 1 (APP/PS1) transgenic mouse models exposed to chronic stress, this intervention can alleviate brain energy deprivation and amyloid-β (Aβ) accumulation, ultimately rescuing depressive-like behaviors and cognitive deficits, offering a promising approach for early prevention and flexible management of AD at high risk of chronic stress.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Silencing
MSR1 in Macrophages Attenuates the Cochlear
Foreign Body Response and Preserves Electrode–Neural Interface
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Cochlear implantation (CI) provides effective auditory rehabilitation for patients with severe-to-profound sensorineural hearing loss. Implantation can nevertheless induce local foreign body response (FBR) and cochlear fibrosis, motivating strategies to reduce tissue reactions and preserve cochlear integrity. Macrophages play a key role in FBR, but their functions are multiple and stage-dependent, and indiscriminate intervention may aggravate cochlear injury. Therefore, more precise strategies are needed to modulate macrophage-mediated FBR after CI. Here, through transcriptomic profiling of cochlear tissues from rats 30 days after cochlear implantation, we identified macrophage scavenger receptor 1 (MSR1) as a prominent signature after CI. In vitro assays further verified the role of MSR1 in reshaping macrophage phenotype and inflammatory activation. To achieve targeted MSR1 regulation in the cochlea, we engineered iRGD-modified extracellular vesicles to deliver siMSR1 (iRGD-EV/siMSR1). iRGD modification enhanced macrophage uptake of EV and enabled efficient siRNA delivery. In a rat CI model, local administration of iRGD-EV/siMSR1 reduced cochlear fibrotic tissue formation and decreased fibrosis-related protein expression. Moreover, iRGD-EV/siMSR1 preserved spiral ganglion neurons and myelin structures, contributing to residual hearing protection after implantation. Early stage analysis at 7 days after implantation showed that iRGD-EV/siMSR1 suppressed macrophage inflammatory activation, reduced TGF-β1-related profibrotic signaling, regulated matrix remodeling, and limited early apoptosis. These findings identify MSR1 as a promising molecular target for cochlear implant-induced FBR and support iRGD-EV/siMSR1 as a potentially translatable strategy for attenuating cochlear fibrosis and preserving the cochlear neural interface, also highlighting the importance of considering neural health when modulating macrophage-mediated responses to cochlear implants.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Nano-Optical Switching
of Photochromic Material through
Ultraviolet and Visible Plasmon Nanofocusing
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Optical control of photochromic properties is essential for optoelectronic devices. The manipulation of such properties has been limited to the microscale because of the wave nature of light; however, scaling down the volume is highly demanded for the future nanosized devices. Herein, we demonstrate optical switching at the nanoscale in an organic photochromic material. Photochromic materials such as diarylethene derivatives exhibit two different states with distinct optical and electronic properties under ultraviolet (UV) and visible light irradiation. We employed plasmon nanofocusing for optical switching of photochromic materials, which allowed the creation of a nanolight source at the apex of a tapered aluminum structure over a broad frequency range. We achieved in situ wavelength control between visible and UV light at the nanoscale for photochromic reactions. Using this technique, we demonstrated nanoscale optical switching between the two states of diarylethene. The switching performance was confirmed for at least nine cycles without degradation. This demonstration would constitute a significant step toward next-generation optoelectronic devices and benefit diverse scientific fields owing to the broad wavelength tunability of plasmon nanofocusing.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
5DSTEM of Liquid-Phase
Nanocrystal Growth Bridges
Ensemble Kinetics and Nanoscale Dynamics
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Resolving how ensemble growth kinetics emerge from particle- and grain-level dynamics is essential for predictive control of nanocrystal synthesis. Here, time-resolved four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4DSTEM), extended into five dimensions (5DSTEM) through continuous acquisition, is used to simultaneously resolve morphology, crystallographic orientation, and lattice strain during Au nanocrystal growth in aqueous HAuCl4. Although ensemble growth follows surface-reaction-limited kinetics, individual nanoparticles exhibit distinct pathways, including continuous growth and discrete coalescence through oriented attachment. These pathways display characteristic orientation dynamics, with stable or gradually selected orientations during continuous growth and abrupt reconfiguration followed by alignment during coalescence. At the ensemble level, the out-of-plane orientation distribution is established early and remains stable, whereas in-plane orientations remain broadly distributed without global alignment. Tensile strain develops progressively from particle surfaces and interfaces, directly linking lattice distortion with evolving morphology and crystallographic structure. By connecting ensemble kinetics with particle- and grain-resolved structural evolution, 5DSTEM provides a general framework for uncovering heterogeneous growth mechanisms and for relating synthesis pathways to structure-dependent properties in functional nanomaterials.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Hybridization State
Engineering of Coal Pitch-Based
Carbon Materials Enabling Ultrastable Aqueous Zinc–Iodine Batteries
with 150,000 Cycles
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Carbon materials with superior porosity and conductivity are widely adopted in aqueous zinc–iodine batteries to host iodine, but suffer from the polyiodide shuttle and cycling stability challenges. Traditional strategies mainly focus on pore structure engineering or heteroatom doping of carbon hosts to confine iodine, but fail to address the sluggish iodine conversion kinetics. Herein, we initially reveal the significant yet overlooked role of hybridization state in reforming the carbon intrinsic activity toward high-efficiency iodine conversion chemistry. With pitch-derived porous carbon as an example, we controllably regulate the C(sp2)/C(sp3) ratio (from 1.23 to 2.21) while maintaining high surface area. These properties lower the activation energy of iodine conversion and effectively suppress the polyiodide shuttle. The zinc–iodine battery exhibits ultrahigh cycling stability after 150,000 cycles and a low self-discharging rate with only 12.5% capacity loss after 20 days. Ah-level pouch cell with 66.6 mgiodine cm–2 achieves a cumulative discharging capacity of 103.51 Ah. The hybridization engineering was successfully extended to commercial porous carbon (YP-50F), prolonging the lifespan from 7425 to 27,000 cycles. This work presents a hybridization state engineering strategy to reform the intrinsic activity of the carbon host to favor the iodine conversion chemistry and beyond.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Frozen
2D Adatom Gas at the Surface of Gold–Copper
Alloys
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Isolated, undercoordinated metal atoms exhibit enhanced reactivity central to catalysis, yet their stabilization on surfaces remains challenging. In heterogeneous single-atom catalysis, activity derives from interactions between individual atoms and a host matrix, but the absence of stabilizing ligands often leads to diffusion, aggregation, and sintering, obscuring structure–activity relationships. On metal surfaces, reactivity is typically limited to sparse, dynamic, undercoordinated sites lining step edges or lattice defects. Here we report a defect-engineering strategy to stabilize isolated adatoms on dilute metal alloy substrates. Scanning tunneling microscopy reveals a high density of uniformly distributed adatoms on Au–Cu(111) terraces that persist under thermal cycling. Combined experiments and modeling attribute this stability to alloy-induced subsurface dislocation networks that trap adatoms and suppress diffusion, forming a two-dimensional frozen gas. These adatoms act as a reactive reservoir, enabling on-surface coordination chemistry inaccessible on pure metals, and providing insights into atomic-scale processes on the surfaces of defect-engineered alloys with implications for heterogeneous catalysis.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Fluorinated Copper(I) Iodine Cluster Scintillators
Enable High-Temperature X-ray Imaging
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The development of scintillators that maintain excellent performance under high temperatures is a critical challenge. Here, by simply replacing the triphenylphosphine ligand with its fluorinated analogue, we successfully switched the emission pathway of Cu2I2 clusters from pure phosphorescence to a hybrid phosphorescence/thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) mechanism, enabling adaptive high-temperature X-ray imaging. Combined experimental and theoretical investigations reveal that the fluorination strategy reduces the singlet–triplet energy gap to an exceptionally small value of 35 meV, thereby promoting efficient reverse intersystem crossing. The TADF contribution reaches 95.7% at room temperature. This temperature-responsive characteristic endows the fluorinated cluster with adaptive X-ray imaging capability across a broad temperature window from 293 to 413 K, overcoming the thermal quenching phenomenon in traditional phosphorescence-only scintillators. This work establishes a molecular design approach for smart scintillators capable of reliable operation in demanding thermal environments.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Electrically Reconfigurable
Silicon Carbide Nanophotonic
Cavities on Thin-Film Lithium Niobate
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Interfacing integrated photonics with solid-state spin defects holds great promise for future quantum networks, but the scaling of spin-photon architectures is hindered by frequency mismatches arising from fabrication-induced variations in photonic cavity resonances and inhomogeneous optical transition frequencies of individual spins. These challenges call for a photonic platform with deterministic and wide-range tunability. Here, we demonstrate a hybrid nanophotonic platform based on direct bonding of silicon carbide photonic crystal nanocavity arrays onto a thin-film lithium niobate-on-insulator, enabling deterministic electrical tuning of multiple SiC nanocavities into mutual spectral resonance. By exploiting the strong electro-optic response of lithium niobate, we achieve continuous and wide-range cavity tuning of 380 GHz (∼1.1 nm), sufficient to compensate both cavity disorder and spin spectral inhomogeneity. The nanocavities balance strong optical confinement with electrical tunability, exhibiting a theoretical Purcell factor of approximately 400. This hybrid platform enables electrically reconfigurable spin-photon interfaces for large-scale integrated quantum photonics.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Micro-LED-Activated
Formaldehyde Sensing via Au Loading-Regulated
Interfacial Engineering in Anatase TiO2 Nanofibers
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Photoactivated metal-oxide gas sensors reduce the energy demand associated with continuous heating, yet selective detection of volatile organic compounds remains constrained by weak electrical transduction and complex surface oxidation pathways. Here, Au-functionalized anatase TiO2 nanofibers (Au/aTiO2 NFs) were integrated with a 395 nm microlight-emitting diode (LED) for low-power formaldehyde (HCHO) sensing. One-pot electrospinning followed by calcination enabled systematic control of Au loading while preserving the anatase nanofiber architecture. Au loading regulated TiO2 crystallite growth, defect states, dispersion, interfacial Au chemical states, and photoexcited carrier relaxation. At 0.15 wt % Au, finely dispersed Au nanoparticles produced a distinct Au/TiO2 interfacial environment and carrier-relaxation behavior, whereas higher loadings induced nanoparticle aggregation and additional nonradiative energy-loss pathways. Under UV micro-LED illumination at 2.63 mW, the optimized sensor exhibited a response of 1093 toward 1 ppm of HCHO, an estimated detection limit of 4.9 ppb, and stable operation over 40 consecutive cycles. Density functional theory calculations further supported the loading-dependent selectivity, showing that changes in the local Au environment selectively modify HCHO adsorption and bond reconstruction. These results identify local Au-site density as a key design parameter governing interfacial reactivity and molecular selectivity in low-power photoactivated gas sensing.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Engineered
Living Materials: A Therapeutic Paradigm
beyond Conventional Biomaterials
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Development of biomaterials in the past two decades has profoundly advanced modern medicine. However, the relatively simple and insufficiently biological functions and lack of self-renewal capability limit their ability to dynamically adapt to complex physiological environments. Engineered living materials (eLMs) use living organisms as core functional units and provide a therapeutic approach for addressing these limitations. Thus, this review systematically summarizes the recent advancements in eLMs, beginning with an overview of the primary biological chassis, including bacteria, microalgae, fungi, and mammalian cells. eLMs hold the valuable capabilities of long-term self-sustainment and self-proliferation within complex biological environments, which are endowed with intelligent regulation. For instance, they can sense environmental signals and execute programmed functional outputs, including therapeutic protein secretion or targeted migration. Moreover, they achieve precise control over therapeutic actions, encompassing spatial localization at the disease site, temporal dynamics of the intervention, and quantitative regulation of outputs. Furthermore, we highlight the broad therapeutic applications of these dynamic systems in addressing complex diseases. Finally, we discuss the current translational challenges and future directions of the field, emphasizing the potential of integrating artificial intelligence with synthetic biology and nanomaterial engineering to develop next-generation programmable eLMs and expand their utility across diverse sectors.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Accelerating the
Discovery of Synthesizable 2D Hybrid
Double Perovskites through Human–LLM Collaborative Descriptor
Engineering
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Two-dimensional hybrid perovskites offer exceptional structural diversity and multifunctional properties, yet their synthesis remains a major bottleneck due to low hit rates and strong reliance on empirical intuition. Here we introduce AL-SynAgent, a human-in-the-loop, ML-guided screening workflow that integrates literature-derived synthetic priors, expert-refined chemical descriptors, and active learning to assess the synthesis feasibility of two dimensional (2D) hybrid organic–inorganic rare-earth double perovskites (HORDPs). By converting LLM-assisted literature knowledge and expert chemical reasoning into system-specific computable descriptors, AL-SynAgent reduces dependence on large experimental data sets while retaining chemically interpretable decision rules. With experimental feedback from only 4.8% of candidate space, the model converged and achieved successful target-phase formation for 11 of the 14 candidates in the prospectively selected experimental set, corresponding to a hit rate of 78.6%. Screening of an enumerated virtual library of 280,000 candidates further prioritized 64,482 compositions with high predicted synthesis feasibility. Notably, three newly obtained compounds also exhibit both excellent ferroelectricity and photoluminescence, including (4-F-321)4RbEu(NO3)8, which displays an exceptionally high Curie temperature of 388 K and strong emission at 592 nm. This work establishes a practical, human-in-the-loop strategy for data-efficient prioritization of candidate compositions within chemically constrained 2D HORDP space under a standardized laboratory synthesis protocol.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Competing Surface
Dynamics of Copper Catalyst Particles
during Electrochemical Carbon Dioxide Reduction
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Copper is a powerful catalyst for the electrochemical carbon dioxide reduction reaction (CO2RR), but it faces challenges with selectivity and stability dependent on its structural characteristics. We developed a platform that combines graphitized carbon nanofibers with identical-location transmission electron microscopy (IL-TEM) to study individual copper nanoparticles at the atomic scale under various reaction conditions. Notably, we observed that competing phenomena such as Ostwald ripening, coalescence, selective etching, and Coulomb-explosion-like fragmentation coexist in the same reaction area, with the latter being qualitatively consistent with a charge-driven fission pathway in larger nanoparticles (&gt;10 nm). By tracking uniquely identifiable nanoparticles both individually and in groups, our findings focus on the range of surface-confined restructuring pathways during CO2RR. This contrasts with solution-mediated phenomena, such as dissolution–precipitation, which dominate under open-circuit potential (OCP) and significantly destabilize the catalyst prior to the reaction, highlighting the importance of eliminating this effect. Under CO2RR conditions, Cu nanoparticles are highly sensitive to subtle variations in the support’s nanotexture, defects, and electronic structure, leading to the coexistence of counteracting mechanisms we observed. These observations provide a structural framework for understanding the dynamic behavior of copper-on-carbon catalysts under CO2RR conditions, guiding the development of strategies to improve catalyst stability and performance.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title: Fluorine-free CO 2  electrolyzer for multicarbon products
content: Renewably powered CO2 electrolysis to multicarbon (C2+) products, including ethanol, offers a route to electrify chemical production, yet high-rate operation relies on fluorinated materials, particularly per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). These materials enable water, ion, and gas management required for efficient ethanol production but persist in the environment, prompting regulations that restrict their use. Attempts to replace PFAS in ionomers and gas diffusion layers (GDLs) have yielded only partial advances, with most candidates facing trade-offs among conductivity, hydrophobicity and chemical durability that limits C2+ production and stability. We thus sought PFAS-free alternatives for each component, beginning with the ionomer, where replacements are challenging due to its role in coordinating CO2, water, and ion transport. To address these requirements, we develop fluorine-free ionic polymer brushes on copper catalysts to decouple these functions. We also fabricate a silicon-polymer-coated GDL that enables 450 hours of stable CO2 reduction operation. Integrating this GDL with the ionic polymer brushes and a sulfonated polyether ether ketone membrane, we demonstrate a fully PFAS-free CO2 electrolyzer for C2+ production, achieving 43% ethanol faradaic efficiency in acidic conditions.
journal: Energy & Environmental Science advanceAccess

title: Interfacial engineering accelerates desolvation kinetics for high-performance alkaline zinc–iron flow batteries
content: Alkaline zinc–iron flow batteries (AZIFBs) are promising candidates for grid-scale energy storage owing to their high cell voltage, intrinsic safety, and compelling cost-effectiveness. Nevertheless, their high-capacity operation is limited by slow interfacial desolvation of zincate ions (Zn(OH)42−), which disrupts ion flux and promotes dendritic deposition and corrosion. Here, we report an anion-chelator-induced interfacial transport channel that accelerates Zn(OH)42− desolvation and regulates zinc deposition. Cyclooctaamylose (COA) serves as a supramolecular scaffold that weakens the Zn–OH solvation shell of incoming Zn(OH)42− and lowers the activation barriers for desolvation and charge transfer. Preferential adsorption of COA on zinc also limits hydroxide uptake, thereby suppressing corrosion and promoting compact deposits. Consequently, these interfacial effects allow AZIFBs to operate at a remarkable areal capacity of 200 mAh cm−2 (at 89% state of charge) with a high coulombic efficiency of 99.0%, while delivering stable operation for over 800 hours at a high capacity of 140 mAh cm−2. Driven by these rapid interfacial kinetics, the battery endures nearly 1200 cycles at an ultra-high current density of 200 mA cm−2 and delivers a power density of 1028 mW cm−2. These results establish targeted interfacial desolvation control as a mechanistically grounded strategy for high-capacity and high-power flow batteries.
journal: Energy & Environmental Science advanceAccess

title: Structure–performance relationships of redox mediators in the lithium–sulfur battery
content: The lithium–sulfur battery is one of the most promising next-generation battery technologies for high-energy applications due to its high gravimetric energy density of 2567 Wh kg−1. Despite its advantages, widespread application of the lithium–sulfur battery has been hindered by poor cycle life and incomplete sulfur utilization. Homogeneous redox mediators (RMs) have emerged as effective additives to enhance the capacity of the battery, yet their mechanistic roles and the links between their molecular properties and cell performance remain poorly understood. Here, we describe the structure–performance relationship of a range of redox mediators in these systems, revealing for the first time the sulfur redox reactions driven by the action of the redox mediators. We show that for quinone-based mediators, the potential of the second reduction is crucial in directing the interconversion between sulfur and lithium sulfide. Our results also demonstrate that mediators are not innocent in degradation processes and can induce parasitic reactions at lithium and/or degrade spontaneously. Incorporation of bulky substituents on the mediator structure enhances operational stability by suppressing these degradation routes. We identify 2,6-di-tert-butyl-1,4-benzoquinone as an especially promising mediator, delivering the greatest performance gains of the quinone-based mediators we studied, and providing a 16% capacity improvement over the standard after 100 cycles. Our mechanistic insights explain this optimal structure–performance relationship and rationalise why previous use of mediators have resulted in poor coulombic inefficiencies. This work enables predictive design of future RMs with improved stability and electrochemical selectivity, and offers a toolbox for rapid evaluation prior to cycling studies.

title: Evaluation of common battery lifetime prediction methods across a variety of public datasets
content: Accurately predicting the lifetime of a given battery could enable much more efficient utilization of deployed batteries and save significant time when testing novel battery designs. Recent studies have demonstrated that machine learning models can be used to predict the lifetime of a battery using early cycle data, but these models are typically only tested on a single dataset. In this work, we evaluate some of these linear and nonlinear models and the features they use on a wide variety of publicly available lithium-ion battery datasets. We also demonstrate how outlier cells can skew model success metrics. For some datasets with a single cell type and at least ten cells, simple linear models can predict cycle life. However, the most informative features and the effect of various algorithmic modifications all vary between datasets. This analysis is intended to provide consistent tools and best practices for a researcher to use any new battery dataset to do data-driven lifetime prediction.

title: The thermal runaway and thermal propagation challenge of lithium-ion batteries: a review of the underlying reactions, released energies and methods for thermal safety improvement
content: Safety aspects are one of the key requirements for the large-scale use of lithium-ion batteries in current and future energy storage systems. This review analyzes the safety-critical mechanisms of thermal runaway and thermal propagation in lithium-ion batteries. At the cell level, the heat-induced decomposition reactions that can trigger thermal runaway are first described in detail and their energy release is investigated. The influence of electrode chemistry, separator design and electrolyte composition on thermal stability is critically evaluated. In addition, systematic explanations are provided on the causes of such reactions, by categorizing them into internal short circuits and abuse conditions (mechanical, thermal, electrical) and analyzing their contribution to local and global heat generation. At the system level, heat transfer mechanisms and the conditions for thermal propagation are discussed. Different classes of thermal barriers are quantitatively compared. Finally, current numerical model approaches for describing thermal runaway and thermal propagation are summarized, and research needs regarding model simplifications and high-quality validation data are identified. The work thus provides a structured basis for the development of targeted safety concepts at the level of electrodes, cells, and battery packs to fulfill future, increasingly stringent, standards and regulatory requirements, also considering alternative cell integration methods.

content:
Sodium‐Ion Batteries
Neutron scattering and imaging techniques are powerful tools to probe structure, morphology, and sodium‐ion dynamics across broad length and time scales. They reveal atomic‐ to mesoscale structural evolution, diffusion pathways, and phase transition mechanisms in sodium‐ion battery materials, deepening insight into electrochemical processes and facilitating the development of high‐performance, and cost‐effective sodium‐ion battery technologies. title: Fabrication of Composite Cathode for All‐Solid‐State Sodium Batteries
content:
The design of composite cathodes for all‐solid‐state sodium batteries must address three critical challenges—interfacial side reactions, interfacial delamination, and highly tortuous transport pathways. This work outlines structural and interfacial strategies to optimize ion transport and mechanical stability, enabling durable, and high‐performance solid‐state sodium battery systems.








Abstract
All‐solid‐state sodium‐ion batteries (ASSSBs) are regarded as highly promising candidates for large‐scale energy storage systems owing to their expected lower cost and enhanced safety. In recent years, the advent of novel fast ion‐conducting solid electrolytes (SEs) has further accelerated the rapid development of this field. Nevertheless, several critical challenges remain, preventing the performance of ASSSBs from surpassing that of their liquid‐electrolyte counterparts. Among these, a key obstacle lies in the design of cathode systems that ensure optimal compatibility between the SE and the cathode active material (CAM). This review focuses on the essential properties and persistent challenges of CAM in ASSSBs employing inorganic SEs and highlights the current strategies developed to address these issues. Particular attention is given to the design considerations at the cathode, particle, and interface levels, including aspects related to the microstructure, mechanical integrity, and (electro)chemical interactions with the SE. Finally, the review outlines future directions and design principles for the development of next‐generation cathode materials in ASSSBs.
